title: NOLA artists, Barefoot and the Atlantic lawsuit
summary: The Wardell Quezergue group on NOLA recorded Barefoot outside Atlantic's first refusal; Atlantic sued Matassa and won, taking over the record.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Well, when you started out, you knew you had a pressing plant and you knew you had this record company. We, did you have artists already lined up? Producers? Or did you have?
Yeah. Sure. And, and of course I, I tracked them as I went along.
Well, who did you have when you started? Who, who was gonna come in? Who was gonna, who did you see?
Well, I, I had the, the, the, the guys that were, were, uh, uh, doing, uh, what did they call themselves? Uh, Wardell and that group. Wardell Cazare? Yeah. And that group. Okay. Yeah.
NOLA.

NOLA. Yeah. And, uh, uh, unfortunately I had a real serious mishap there. Uh, they were getting money from Atlantic Records. Atlantic had. Develop money. Right. Develop money. Right. And, and the idea was that they would do records. And Atlantic would have first refusal.
They would have a first refusal. Right.

Well, Atlantic kept first refusing a whole bunch of stuff. So they, so a couple of them got ticked off. Said, well, we're gonna, we're gonna do something on the side without them. That turned out to be barefoot.
Now, did they send that to, to?
No. They didn't send it? No. They, they gave it to us directly.
So Atlantic never had any chance to refuse?

And I never had a chance on it. And there's a gray area about whether they really were separate. The guys that did barefoot and were really separate from the other people and not, I, I can't argue about that. But I, I'll tell you what I can tell you is Atlantic sued me and ultimately won.
Well, it sued you? Me. Why?
Because it said I had no right to direct it.
But it was on the NOLA label, wasn't it? If I recall. Yeah. It was on NOLA, it wasn't on, which, which wasn't you.

But I had the national distribution. You had national distribution. Right. I leased it from there. Okay. Anyway, they ultimately prevailed and the reason they prevailed was we, we were in court over it and I'm spending, nobody else was spending money on a lawyer. I was. Two of the guys involved in that literally went to Atlantic and made a deal. Said, look, we'll say it's yours and, you know, if you, if you, you know, do this or that for us. And they did. And that was the end of that. And so. Who were these two individuals? Let's not talk about that. I don't want to name people. Because I think they did it out of weakness, not out of meanness.
Was Jerry Wexler involved with this suit?

Well, Wexler and, and, and, and Ahmet were, were, you know, it was kind of strange, you know. We were, we were, we were always good friends and all that, but we had this battle going on. We'd get on the phone and they'd tell me, you know, this thing is ours. You know, and I said, no, no, it's mine. You know, I mean, we, we, we were talking about it on the phone, you know. And saying, hey, they're not, not as lawyer to lawyer, but as person to person. And, and, and, and, and they said, well, you know, we're going to put our house council on it because we believe, you know. And that was the end of that. And, and all, like I say, ultimately they prevailed. And that was it.
So you were students in, in federal court or?
I don't remember which. It doesn't make a lot of difference. Federal court probably, yeah. Oh. Yeah. And I lost that. I, you know, I had to cave in on that one. Yeah.
So what happened? Did Atlantic took over distribution?
Took over everything, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. But it was a finished thing by then.
Yeah, but it was already in the charts.
Oh yeah. Oh yeah.
At the time.
It was a, it was, it had finished its first run of, of popularity. Yeah.
Mm-hmm. Yeah, by the time they would see it.
Mm-hmm.
